Section 1.  Of the Nature of Flatland



I call our world Flatland, not because we call it so, but to make its
nature clearer to you, my happy readers, who are privileged to live in
Space.

Imagine a vast sheet of paper on which straight Lines, Triangles,
Squares, Pentagons, Hexagons, and other figures, instead of remaining
fixed in their places, move freely about, on or in the surface, but
without the power of rising above or sinking below it, very much like
shadows--only hard and with luminous edges--and you will then have a
pretty correct notion of my country and countrymen.  Alas, a few years
ago, I should have said "my universe":  but now my mind has been opened
to higher views of things.

In such a country, you will perceive at once that it is impossible that
there should be anything of what you call a "solid" kind; but I dare
say you will suppose that we could at least distinguish by sight the
Triangles, Squares, and other figures, moving about as I have described
them.  On the contrary, we could see nothing of the kind, not at least
so as to distinguish one figure from another.  Nothing was visible, nor
could be visible, to us, except Straight Lines; and the necessity of
this I will speedily demonstrate.

Place a penny on the middle of one of your tables in Space; and leaning
over it, look down upon it.  It will appear a circle.

But now, drawing back to the edge of the table, gradually lower your
eye (thus bringing yourself more and more into the condition of the
inhabitants of Flatland), and you will find the penny becoming more and
more oval to your view, and at last when you have placed your eye
exactly on the edge of the table (so that you are, as it were, actually
a Flatlander) the penny will then have ceased to appear oval at all,
and will have become, so far as you can see, a straight line.

The same thing would happen if you were to treat in the same way a
Triangle, or Square, or any other figure cut out of pasteboard.  As
soon as you look at it with your eye on the edge on the table, you will
find that it ceases to appear to you a figure, and that it becomes in
appearance a straight line.  Take for example an equilateral
Triangle--who represents with us a Tradesman of the respectable class.
Fig. 1 represents the Tradesman as you would see him while you were
bending over him from above; figs. 2 and 3 represent the Tradesman, as
you would see him if your eye were close to the level, or all but on
the level of the table; and if your eye were quite on the level of the
table (and that is how we see him in Flatland) you would see nothing
but a straight line.

When I was in Spaceland I heard that your sailors have very similar
experiences while they traverse your seas and discern some distant
island or coast lying on the horizon.  The far-off land may have bays,
forelands, angles in and out to any number and extent; yet at a
distance you see none of these (unless indeed your sun shines bright
upon them revealing the projections and retirements by means of light
and shade), nothing but a grey unbroken line upon the water.

Well, that is just what we see when one of our triangular or other
acquaintances comes toward us in Flatland.  As there is neither sun
with us, nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows, we have none
of the helps to the sight that you have in Spaceland.  If our friend
comes closer to us we see his line becomes larger; if he leaves us it
becomes smaller:  but still he looks like a straight line; be he a
Triangle, Square, Pentagon, Hexagon, Circle, what you will--a straight
Line he looks and nothing else.

You may perhaps ask how under these disadvantageous circumstances we
are able to distinguish our friends from one another: but the answer to
this very natural question will be more fitly and easily given when I
come to describe the inhabitants of Flatland.  For the present let me
defer this subject, and say a word or two about the climate and houses
in our country.

DEDICATION

Dear Mr. Way,

_After so many letters to people who never existed, may I venture a short one, to a person very real to me, though I have never seen him, and only know him by his many kindnesses? Perhaps you will add another to these by accepting the Dedication of a little work, of a sort experimental in English, and in prose, though Horace--in Latin and in verse--was successful with it long ago_?

_Very sincerely yours_,

_A. LANG_.

_To W. J. Way_, _Esq_. _Topeka_, _Kansas_.

PREFACE

These Letters were originally published in the _Independent_ of New York. The idea of writing them occurred to the author after he had produced "Letters to Dead Authors." That kind of Epistle was open to the objection that nobody _would_ write so frankly to a correspondent about his own work, and yet it seemed that the form of Letters might be attempted again. The _Lettres a Emilie sur la Mythologie_ are a well- known model, but Emilie was not an imaginary correspondent. The persons addressed here, on the other hand, are all people of fancy--the name of Lady Violet Lebas is an invention of Mr. Thackeray's: gifted Hopkins is the minor poet in Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes's "Guardian Angel." The author's object has been to discuss a few literary topics with more freedom and personal bias than might be permitted in a graver kind of essay. The Letter on Samuel Richardson is by a lady more frequently the author's critic than his collaborator.

INTRODUCTORY: OF MODERN ENGLISH POETRY

_To Mr. Arthur Wincott, Topeka, Kansas_.

Dear Wincott,--You write to me, from your "bright home in the setting sun," with the flattering information that you have read my poor "Letters to Dead Authors." You are kind enough to say that you wish I would write some "Letters to Living Authors;" but that, I fear, is out of the question,--for me.

She sat at her mahogany desk, the heavy scent of beeswax and damp wool filling the room, her gaze fixed upon the thick sheaf of letters that had arrived by the morning post. They were from Mr. Andrew Lang, his sprawling, confident script detailing his latest thoughts on literature.

Violet sighed, tracing the edge of the parchment with a silver letter-opener. Lang was a man of undeniable erudition, yet his letters were suffocated by the very patriarchal complacency she so deeply despised. He wrote to her of Virgil, of modern English poetry, of Fielding and Rochefoucauld, positioning himself as the benevolent instructor to her "undefeated resolution to admire only the right things."

"The right things," she murmured aloud, the words tasting like ash. What he meant, of course, was the established canon—the texts elevated by centuries of wealthy, privileged men who saw their own reflections in the exploits of conquerors and the musings of comfortable philosophers.

She turned to his pages on Fielding. Lang excused the novelist's coarse morality, arguing that men must be pardoned the "vices of young blood" so long as they were brave and generous. He painted a nostalgic picture of a "lusty old militant world," entirely blind to the fact that this merry England was built upon the bruised backs of women and the indentured silence of the poor. He dismissed the systemic inequalities that left women like Sophia Western with no recourse but to forgive the betrayals of their husbands.

[Reference Original]: Under certain circumstances there are few hours in life more agreeable than the hour dedicated to the ceremony known as afternoon tea.

There are circumstances in which, whether you partake of the tea or not--some people of course never do,--the situation is in itself delightful.

Those that I have in mind in beginning to unfold this simple history offered an admirable setting to an innocent pastime.

The implements of the little feast had been disposed upon the lawn of an old English country-house, in what I should call the perfect middle of a splendid summer afternoon.

Part of the afternoon had waned, but much of it was left, and what was left was of the finest and rarest quality.

Real dusk would not arrive for many hours; but the flood of summer light had begun to ebb, the air had grown mellow, the shadows were long upon the smooth, dense turf.

They lengthened slowly, however, and the scene expressed that sense of leisure still to come which is perhaps the chief source of one's enjoyment of such a scene at such an hour.

From five o'clock to eight is on certain occasions a little eternity; but on such an occasion as this the interval could be only an eternity of pleasure.

The persons concerned in it were taking their pleasure quietly, and they were not of the sex which is supposed to furnish the regular votaries of the ceremony I have mentioned.

The shadows on the perfect lawn were straight and angular; they were the shadows of an old man sitting in a deep wicker-chair near the low table on which the tea had been served, and of two younger men strolling to and fro, in desultory talk, in front of him.

The old man had his cup in his hand; it was an unusually large cup, of a different pattern from the rest of the set and painted in brilliant colours.

He disposed of its contents with much circumspection, holding it for a long time close to his chin, with his face turned to the house.
[Reference Rewrite]: There are certain hours in life that exist suspended outside the relentless machinery of time, offering an illusion of grace against the void. The ritual known as afternoon tea is one such pantomime—a quiet rebellion, perhaps, or merely an opiate for the idle class. The staging for this particular iteration of the ceremony was almost absurdly idyllic, laid out upon the manicured lawn of an English country estate in the deep, golden bruised light of a late summer afternoon. The shadows of the great oaks stretched across the turf like the dark, reaching fingers of history itself, pointing toward a dusk that seemed perpetually deferred. To exist in such an interval, from five o'clock to eight, was to inhabit an eternity of curated leisure—a luxury purchased by invisible, grinding labor elsewhere, but enjoyed here with a placid, unquestioning serenity.

Three figures occupied this velvet stage. The geometry of their arrangement was anchored by an old man seated in a deep wicker chair, nursing an unusually large, brilliantly painted teacup. The cup was raised to his chin with the trembling circumspection of one who understands the fragility of the body. Before him paced two younger men, moving through the thick, amber air in desultory orbits, their cigarettes leaving thin trails of smoke that dissolved into the canopy of ancient leaves. Behind them rose the house, a red-brick Tudor monolith of gables and clustered chimneys, smothered in ivy. It was a structure heavy with the ghosts of monarchs and the violence of Cromwell’s wars, ultimately commodified, sanitized, and purchased at a ruthless bargain by the old man in the chair—an American banker who had converted the blood and mud of English history into an aesthetic asset.

I call our world Flatland, not because we possess a name for it, but to strip away the confusion of higher dimensions and reveal its stark, two-dimensional truth to you, my fortunate readers dwelling in the boundless expanse of Space. Envision a vast, infinite plane of paper where straight lines, triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, and myriad other geometric forms drift freely across the surface, trapped within its confines, unable to rise above or sink beneath it. These shapes exist like shadows cast by solid objects, yet unlike mere phantoms, they are tangible, possessing hardness and luminous edges. This is the essence of my nation and its citizens. Once, in ignorance, I might have termed this realm "my universe"; but since my mind has been illuminated by superior perspectives, I reserve that grander title for the dimension beyond ours.

In such a realm, the concept of "solidity" is an impossibility, a phantom notion borrowed from your world. One might reasonably assume that despite this lack of depth, we could visually distinguish between a triangle, a square, or any other polygon as they moved about. Yet, this assumption is fundamentally flawed. We cannot see figures as you understand them; we perceive nothing but straight lines. Let me demonstrate this necessity with a simple experiment. Place a copper penny upon the center of a table in your three-dimensional space. Now, lean over it and gaze downward. To your eyes, the coin appears a perfect circle. Draw back until your eye rests at the table's edge, gradually lowering your vision until you align perfectly with the surface, mimicking the condition of a Flatlander. At this precise moment, the penny loses its circular guise, elongating into an increasingly narrow oval until, finally, it resolves into a single, unbroken straight line. This phenomenon holds true for any shape cut from pasteboard—a triangle, a square, or a complex polygon. When viewed from directly above the plane, the figure vanishes, replaced solely by its linear boundary.

Consider, for instance, an equilateral triangle, which among us signifies a tradesman of respectable standing. From your vantage point high above, he presents as a distinct geometric form. As your eye descends, approaching the level of the tabletop, the figure distorts, shrinking in height while widening in breadth. Finally, when your eye lies flush with the surface—as it does for every inhabitant of Flatland—you behold nothing but a straight line. No corners, no vertices, no internal angles are visible to us; only the line remains.

This experience mirrors the plight of your sailors traversing the oceans. When they gaze upon a distant island or coastline on the horizon, the intricate geography—bays, headlands, and recessions—is lost to distance. Unless the sun strikes the land with brilliance, casting shadows that reveal relief, the sailor sees only a grey, unbroken line cutting across the water. So too do we observe our neighbors. Without a sun to cast shadows, and lacking the third dimension to provide cues of depth, we rely solely on the length of the line before us. If a triangular acquaintance approaches, his line grows longer; if he departs, it shrinks. Whether he is a triangle, a square, a pentagon, a hexagon, or even a circle, to our eyes, he is indistinguishable from any other straight line.

You may rightly wonder how we navigate this visual deprivation, distinguishing friend from foe amidst a sea of identical lines. The answer to this profound mystery requires a deeper understanding of our physiology and social codes, a topic I shall address when describing the inhabitants themselves. For now, let us turn our attention to the climate and architecture of our peculiar country.
